column2: The fifth prefatory discussion: on the differences in the conditions of civilization with regard to plenty and hunger, and the effects that arise from this on the bodies and characters of human beings

Know that not all of these temperate zones have plenty, and not all their inhabitants live in ease. Rather, some of them provide their people with a plentiful living, in grains, condiments, wheat and fruits, because of the fertility of the growing grounds, the balance of the clay and the abundance of civilization; and some of them have bare land that grows no crops and no herbage at all, so that their inhabitants live in hardship, such as the people of the Hijaz and the south of Yemen, and such as the Veiled People (al-Mulaththamūn) of Ṣanhāja, who live in the desert of the Maghrib and the fringes of the sands between the Berbers and the Sudan. For these people lack grains and condiments altogether; their foods and sustenance are only milk and meat. So too the Arabs who roam the wastelands: for although they obtain grains and condiments from the Tells (al-tulūl), that happens only now and then, under the yoke of the Tells’ garrison, and in small quantities because of their scarcity of means, so that they cannot get from it enough to meet their need, or even come near it, let alone ease and plenty. You find them confining themselves, in most of their circumstances, to milk, which makes up for wheat for them in the best possible way. And yet you find these people of the wastelands, who lack grains and condiments, in better condition in their bodies and characters than the people of the Tells who are steeped in the good life: their complexions are clearer, their bodies purer, their shapes more perfect and more handsome, their characters further from deviation, and their minds sharper in knowledge and perception. This is a matter to which experience bears witness in every generation of them. So great is the difference between the Arabs

and the Berbers in the respects we have described, and between the Veiled People and the people of the Tells. Whoever has experienced this knows it. The reason for this, and God knows best, is that the abundance of food and the abundance of corrupt, putrid humors and their moistures generate in the body bad residues, from which arises an extension of the body’s dimensions out of all proportion. This is followed by a dimming of complexions and an ugliness of shapes from the abundance of flesh, as we have said; and the moistures cover over minds and thoughts through the bad vapors from them that rise to the brain, so that there come dullness, heedlessness and, in general, deviation from balance. Consider this in the animals of the wastelands and the lands of dearth, such as gazelles, ostriches, oryxes, giraffes, wild asses and cattle, together with their like among the animals of the Tells, the farmlands and the fertile pastures: how you find a great gulf between them in the clearness of their skins, the beauty of their sheen and shapes, the proportion of their limbs and the keenness of their faculties of perception. The gazelle is the brother of the goat, the giraffe is the brother of the camel, and the [wild] ass and cattle are brothers of the [domestic] ass and cattle, and the difference between them is what you have seen. This is only because plenty in the Tells has produced in the bodies of these animals such bad residues and corrupt humors that its effect shows on them, whereas hunger has made the build and shapes of the animals of the wastelands as fine as it pleased. Consider this in human beings too: we find that the people of zones where living is plentiful, rich in crops, livestock, condiments and fruits, are generally characterized by dullness in their minds and coarseness in their bodies.

And this is the case with the Berbers who are steeped in condiments and wheat, compared with those of them who live austerely and confine themselves to barley or sorghum, such as the Maṣāmida among them and the people of Ghumāra and al-Sūs: you find these better off in their intellects and bodies. Likewise the people of the lands of the Maghrib in general, who are steeped in condiments and wheat, compared with the people of al-Andalus, in whose land clarified butter is entirely lacking and whose living is mostly sorghum: you find in the people of al-Andalus a keenness of intellect, a lightness of body and a readiness to accept instruction that are not found in others. Likewise the people of the outlying districts of the Maghrib in general, compared with the settled people and the people of the cities. For although the city people, like them, use condiments in abundance and live in plenty, they use them only after treating them by cooking and refining them with what they mix with them, so that their coarseness goes away and their consistency is made thin. Most of their food is mutton and chicken, and among the condiments they do not prize clarified butter, because of its insipidity. So for this reason moistures are fewer in their foods, and the bad residues that these bring to their bodies are lighter. That is why you find the bodies of the city people more delicate than the bodies of the desert people who live roughly. Likewise you find that those of the desert people who are accustomed to hunger have no residues in their bodies, either thick or fine.

Know that the effect of this plenty on the body and its conditions appears even in the state of religion and worship. We find that those who live austerely, among the desert people or the settled people, and who discipline themselves to hunger and to keeping away from pleasures, are better in religion and more devoted to worship than people of luxury and plenty. Indeed, we find the people of religion few in towns and cities, because of the hardness of heart and the heedlessness that pervade them, bound up with overeating of meats, condiments and the choicest part of the wheat; and for this reason devout worshippers and ascetics are found only among those who are austere in their food, among the desert people. Likewise we find that these people who live in plenty and are steeped in its good things, whether among the desert people or among the settled people and the people of the cities, are quicker than others to perish when the lean years come upon them and famines seize them, such as the Berbers of the Maghrib and the people of the city of Fez and of Egypt, according to what reaches us; and they are not like the Arabs of the wastelands and the desert, nor like the people of the date-palm lands, whose living is mostly dates, nor like the people of Ifrīqiya at this time, whose living is mostly barley and olive oil, nor like the people of al-Andalus, whose living is mostly sorghum and olive oil. For although the lean years and famines seize these, they do not strike them as they strike those, and death from hunger does not become frequent among them; indeed, it does not even occur in rare cases. The reason for this, and God knows best, is that those who are steeped in plenty and accustomed to condiments, and especially clarified butter, have intestines that acquire from this a moisture

over and above their original constitutional moisture, until it exceeds its limit. Then, when their habit is contravened by a scarcity of provisions, the absence of condiments and the use of coarse food they are not used to, dryness and contraction come quickly to the intestine, which is extremely weak; so disease quickly reaches it, and its owner dies suddenly, because it is one of the vital parts. Those who perish in famines are therefore killed only by the habitual, earlier satiety, not by the later, newly arrived hunger. As for those who are accustomed to few condiments and little clarified butter, their original moisture stays at its limit without increase, and it is receptive to all natural foods, so that no dryness or deviation occurs in their intestines when foods change, and they are generally safe from the destruction that befalls others through plenty and an abundance of condiments in their food. The basis of all this is that you should know that foods, and becoming familiar with them or leaving them, are only a matter of habit. Whoever has accustomed himself to a food, and taking it suits him, finds it familiar, and leaving it and changing to another becomes a sickness, so long as it does not stray altogether from the purpose of food, as poisons, spurges and whatever is extremely deviant do. But as for what is found to have nourishment and suitability in it,

it becomes a food made familiar by habit. So if a person trains himself to use milk and vegetables in place of wheat until this becomes his regular practice, then that has become food for him, and he does without wheat and grains, without doubt. So too with someone who accustoms himself to endure hunger and to do without food, as is reported of the people of spiritual exercises; for we hear strange reports about them on this matter, which anyone unfamiliar with them would almost deny. The cause of this is habit: when the soul grows familiar with something, it becomes part of its disposition and nature, because the soul is highly changeable. So when it has become accustomed to hunger, by gradual stages and through spiritual exercise, this has become a natural habit for it. What the physicians imagine, that hunger is deadly, is not as they imagine, except when the soul is made to bear it all at once and food is cut off from it entirely; for then the intestine closes up and is afflicted by a sickness with which death is to be feared. But if that extent is reached gradually and as a spiritual exercise, by reducing food little by little, as the Sufis do, it is far from destruction. This gradual approach is necessary even in giving up this spiritual exercise: if one is returned all at once to the first food, death is feared for him, and he must be brought back only gradually, just as he began in the exercise. And we have indeed seen someone who endures hunger for forty days of continuous fasting, and more.

And our teachers were present at the session of Sultan Abū al-Ḥasan, when two women, from Algeciras and Ronda, were brought before him, who had kept themselves from eating altogether for years. Their case had become widely known and they were put to the test, and their situation proved genuine and remained so until they died. We have also seen many of our companions who confined themselves to the milk of a she-goat, taking its teat in the mouth at some time of the day or at the breaking of the fast, and made that their food, and kept on with it for fifteen years; and there are many others, and this is not to be dismissed as strange. Know that hunger is better for the body than an abundance of foods in every respect, for anyone who can manage it, or can manage to reduce food; and it has an effect on bodies and intellects, in their clarity and soundness, as we have said. Consider this from the effects that foods produce in bodies: we have seen that those who feed on the meat of superb animals of great bulk have generations that grow up the same way, and this is observed in the desert people as compared with the settled people. So too with those who feed on camels’ milk and meat, together with what it impresses on their characters of patience, endurance and the ability to carry heavy loads, which is found in camels; and their intestines also grow up in the likeness of camels’ intestines in soundness and thickness, so that weakness does not come upon them

and what reaches others from the circulation of foods does not reach them. So they drink spurges to loosen their bowels, undisguised, such as colocynth before it is cooked, dīryās and qarbiyūn, and no harm comes to their intestines from them; whereas if the settled people, whose intestines are delicate from the fine foods on which they were raised, took these, destruction would come to them faster than the blink of an eye, because of the poison in them. Among the effects of foods on bodies is also what the people of agriculture have mentioned and the people of experience have observed: that if hens are fed on grains cooked in camel dung, and their eggs are taken and then brooded on, the chickens that come from them are as large as can be. They may even dispense with feeding the hens and cooking the grains, by putting that dung in with the eggs being brooded, and then their chickens come out extremely large. There are many examples like this. So if we see these effects of foods on bodies, there is no doubt that hunger too has effects on bodies, because two opposites stand on the same footing with regard to having an effect and not having one. So the effect of hunger lies in the purity of bodies from corrupt excesses and mixed moistures that impair the body and the intellect, just as food has an effect in the existence of that body. And God is all-encompassing in His knowledge.
